title: Add, update, delete keys
blurb: Assigning to an existing key updates it, assigning to a new key inserts it, del removes it, and [] on a missing key raises KeyError.

notes.1: A dictionary with four key → value pairs. Keys 1–4 are the labels, the strings are the values.
notes.2: Key 3 already exists, so assignment UPDATES its value. The dictionary does not grow.
notes.3: Key 5 is new, so assignment INSERTS a new pair at the end. The dictionary now has 5 entries.
notes.4: del removes key 2 together with its value. The remaining pairs keep their order.
notes.5: print shows the dictionary as it is now: 4 entries in insertion order.
notes.6: Key 9 was never inserted, so lookup with [] raises KeyError. Use .get(9) to avoid the error.

title: Looping over a dictionary
blurb: A plain for loop over a dictionary hands out the KEYS, one per pass; D1[key] fetches the value.

notes.2: The loop takes the next KEY from the dictionary and stores it in key. Values are not handed out.
notes.3: D1[key] looks the value up from the key, and print shows both.

title: Looping with items()
blurb: items() yields (key, value) pairs; unpacking them in the for header gives both names without a second lookup.

notes.2: items() hands out one (key, value) tuple per pass; the loop unpacks it into key and value.

title: get() vs setdefault()
blurb: get() only reads. setdefault() reads AND inserts the key when it is missing. [] raises KeyError.

notes.2: get(5) returns None because key 5 is missing, and d1 is NOT changed.
notes.3: get(5, 'Missing') returns the supplied default instead of None. d1 is still unchanged.
notes.4: Key 3 exists, so setdefault(3) just returns its value, 'Three'. Nothing is inserted.
notes.5: Key 5 is missing, so setdefault inserts it with the default None. d1 grows.
notes.6: Key 6 is missing: it is inserted with the value you supplied, 'Undefined'.
notes.7: Key 7 was never inserted, so [] raises KeyError (get and setdefault would not).

title: update() merges
blurb: update() copies every pair of another dictionary in: new keys are added, existing keys are overwritten.

notes.1: The dictionary that will receive the new pairs.
notes.2: d2 shares key 4 with d1 and brings a new key 5.
notes.3: Key 4 already exists in d1, so its value is OVERWRITTEN; key 5 is new, so it is ADDED. d2 is untouched.

title: fromkeys() and the shared list trap
blurb: dict.fromkeys(keys, value) gives every key the SAME value object - harmless for numbers and strings, a trap for lists.

notes.1: Three keys to build a dictionary from.
notes.2: No second argument, so every value is None.
notes.3: Every key gets the same default string. Strings are immutable, so sharing is harmless.
notes.4: ONE empty list is created and every key points to that same list.
notes.5: Appending through key 1 changes the single shared list, so keys 2 and 3 'see' it too.
notes.6: All three values show ['x']. Use {k: [] for k in l1} to get a separate list per key.

title: Alias vs copy() (shallow copy)
blurb: d2 = d1 is a second NAME for the same dictionary. d1.copy() is a new dictionary, but nested mutable values are still shared.

notes.1: Key 3 holds a list, which is a mutable object.
notes.2: No copy is made: d2 is simply another name for the same dictionary object.
notes.3: copy() builds a NEW dictionary with its own pairs, but the list under key 3 is the SAME list (shallow copy).
notes.4: Rebinding key 1 in d3 only touches d3. d1 and d2 keep 'One'.
notes.5: The list under key 3 is one shared object, so d1, d2 and d3 all see 'c'.
notes.6: d2 is an alias of d1, so the new key appears in d1 as well, but not in the independent copy d3.

title: pop, popitem, del, clear
blurb: pop(key) removes by key, popitem() removes the last pair, del removes by key, clear() empties everything.

notes.2: pop(2) removes key 2 and returns its value, 'Two'.
notes.3: Key 5 is absent, so the supplied default is returned and the dictionary is unchanged.
notes.4: popitem() removes the most recently inserted pair and returns it as a (key, value) tuple.
notes.5: del d1[1] removes the pair and returns nothing.
notes.6: clear() empties the dictionary in place; d1 is still the same object, just with no pairs.
notes.7: Without a default, pop on a missing key raises KeyError.

title: Comprehension = loop + filter
blurb: {x: y for x, y in l1 if x % 2 == 0} does exactly what this loop does: unpack, test, insert.

notes.2: Start with an empty dictionary; a comprehension builds this for you.
notes.3: Unpack the next tuple into x and y (the 'for x, y in ...' part of the comprehension).
notes.4: The filter: only even keys pass (the 'if ...' part of the comprehension).
notes.5: Reached only when the filter is true: the pair is inserted.

title: Invert a Dictionary
blurb: Swap keys and values. Several keys can share a value, so each new value is a SET of original keys.

notes.1: Six pairs; values 1, 2 and 3 are shared by several keys.
notes.2: An empty dictionary for the inverted result.
notes.3: Take the next (key, value) pair of the original.
notes.4: Has this VALUE already been seen as a key of the inverted dictionary?
notes.5: Yes: add the original key to the existing set.
notes.7: No: create a new one-element set holding the key.
notes.8: Every original key now sits in the set of its value.
